Appendix A Experimental Details

Simulated benchmarks. LIBERO has four suites (Object, Spatial, Goal, and Long) with 10 tasks each and 50 demonstrations per task. One model is trained on all 40 tasks and evaluated on each suite separately. LIBERO-plus perturbs the camera, the initial robot pose, the object layout, the background, the lighting, and the sensor noise. π0.5\pi_{0.5} and ImageWAM are tested on LIBERO and on a shared set of 2008 LIBERO-plus instances, which also perturb the language instruction.

Single-arm robot tasks. All four tasks on the Franka Research 3 arm use multiple cameras, and the actions are joint angles. In the box task, the arm puts a mango into a box and then closes the lid. Its 40 demonstrations are collected with a SpaceMouse through the HIL-SERL teleoperation framework (Luo et al., 2025). In the key task, the arm grasps a key and hangs it on a hook of a wooden key holder, learned from 40 demonstrations collected in the same way. In the sock task, the arm takes a sock from the top of a small cabinet, folds it on the table, puts it into the open drawer, and closes the drawer, learned from 40 demonstrations. In the insertion task, the arm grasps a blue block and inserts it into a matching hole of a black board, learned from 40 demonstrations. Inference times on this robot are measured on one RTX 5080.

Dual-arm robot tasks. All tasks on the dual-arm and dexterous-hand robots use joint angles as actions at 15 Hz. In the flower insertion task, one arm of the Galaxea R1 Lite grasps a long-stemmed poppy or a short-stemmed dahlia from a glass vase and inserts its thin stem into the narrow opening of another vase, so a small error of the gripper pose makes the stem miss the opening. One model is trained on both flowers from 95 demonstrations (38 poppy and 57 dahlia), with a head and a wrist camera. In the microwave task, one arm grasps a bowl of corn, places it in the microwave, and pushes it in, and the other arm then closes the door. It is learned from 34 demonstrations, with a head and two wrist cameras. In the two-flower task, one arm inserts two flowers one after the other into the same vase, learned from 95 demonstrations. In the drawer task, one arm puts an apple from the top of a cabinet into its open drawer, and the other arm closes the drawer. The demonstrations contain both assignments of the arms, 25 with the left arm and 25 with the right arm placing the apple, with a head and two wrist cameras.

Dexterous-hand tasks. The policy runs at 15 Hz, and each predicted chunk is linearly interpolated to 60 Hz joint position targets for the arm and the 22 joints of each hand. In the can task, the Sharpa North robot picks up a can with its Sharpa hand and places it on a plate, learned from 50 demonstrations. In the cup task, the hand picks up a fallen cup, reorients it, and places it upright. Its 50 demonstrations are drawn at random from the reorient_cup_upright task of the public SharpaDex dataset (Sharpa Robotics, 2026), recorded by Sharpa in another lab, and the policies are tested in our lab with other cups and another background. In the pill task, the two hands pour pills from one cup into another and put both cups back. Its 50 demonstrations are those of one recording session of the transfer_pills_between_cups task of SharpaDex closest to our placement of the cups, and the policies are tested with cups of other colors. In the stacking task, the hand stacks a red cube on a green cube. Its 50 demonstrations come from the stack_cube task of SharpaDex, and the policies are tested in our lab with colored cubes instead of the wooden cubes of the demonstrations.

Humanoid tasks. The Unitree G1 humanoid with two Inspire DFX dexterous hands is controlled through GR00T N1.7 (Bjorck et al., 2025). As in ImageWAM, ODE policy reads the condition from GR00T once per chunk. A vector field of about 5M parameters, fine-tuned on top of GR00T, integrates chunks of H=16H=16 steps with Euler, with the diversity head as in all IL experiments. The baseline is the original action head of GR00T N1.7.

Visuomotor policies. All methods share the same observation encoder, a ResNet-18 (He et al., 2016) with group normalization (Wu and He, 2018) and random cropping that encodes the last 8 image frames, and a CLIP text embedding (Radford et al., 2021) of the instruction. Except in the model-size study, the parameters outside the encoder are matched to about 24M (ODE-MLP 24.40M, ODE-DiT 24.15M, FM-DiT 23.93M, and the others within 5%). All methods are trained with AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019), learning rate 10−410^{-4}, batch size 32, and a cosine schedule defined over 100 epochs, and shorter runs stop early under the same schedule. The model-size study changes the width of the action head, with 4 layers for both methods. For the 1.5M ODE policy, the network that maps the observation features to the condition is also narrowed (condition width 136 instead of 512), since it alone has 4.2M parameters at the default width. Each visuomotor experiment is run with three random seeds, except ODE-DiT with one seed. The data-efficiency study changes only the number of demonstrations per task, so fewer demonstrations also mean fewer gradient steps per epoch.

ODE policy. The vector field is a 4-layer FiLM-MLP of width 1732 that takes the action state and the proprioception as input and is modulated by the condition. It corresponds to the conditional residual block of the 1D UNet of FM-UNet and DDPM-UNet without the temporal convolution, since the field takes a single state rather than a sequence of actions, and we therefore call it ODE-MLP in the tables. ODE-DiT replaces it with AdaLN Transformer blocks of width 512 and 4 layers (Appendix B.8). The state is the desired action of the LIBERO operational space controller, i.e., the current pose plus 0.05 m and 0.5 rad times the normalized command, so that a unit tracking gain reproduces the demonstrated command exactly. Each chunk of 8 steps is integrated with RK4 at 20 Hz. Half of the training segments are perturbed by about 1 cm and 0.03 rad with ρ=0.7\rho=0.7. The diversity head has K=12K=12 components. LIBERO uses the component means and the navigation task samples them. The binary gripper is predicted by a separate head.

Baselines. FM-DiT, FM-UNet, DDPM-DiT, and DDPM-UNet predict chunks of 8 actions with the DiT or the 1D UNet head of the corresponding generative model. A2A-DiT starts its flow from the history of actions, perturbed by Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.5. ACT uses its CVAE Transformer decoder. FM-DiT and FM-UNet integrate their flow with 10 midpoint steps, i.e., 20 network calls per chunk, DDPM-DiT and DDPM-UNet denoise in 100 steps, and A2A-DiT generates a chunk in one flow step. As for ODE policy, every baseline reads the last 8 image frames, predicts a chunk of 8 actions, and executes all of them before the next observation.

Evaluation and metrics. Each LIBERO checkpoint runs 20 episodes for each of the 10 tasks of each suite from the fixed initial states of the benchmark. Execution quality is measured on the successful episodes. The jerk is the RMS jerk of the measured end-effector position. The in-chunk and cross-chunk smoothness are the mean change of the command between consecutive steps inside a chunk and at the first step of a new chunk, and their quotient is the boundary ratio. The completion time is the number of control steps. Inference times in the main text are measured during these evaluations on shared GPUs, and times on one idle RTX 4090 are reported in Table S1. LIBERO-plus samples 50 instances per perturbation type and suite with the same sampling seed for all methods.

Appendix B Additional Results

B.1 Execution Quality

Table S1 repeats the timing of Fig. 7(A) on one idle RTX 4090, and the ranking stays the same. With RK4, ODE policy takes 8.82 ms per call, 4.8 times less than FM-DiT and 38 times less than DDPM-UNet, and only the single-pass ACT and A2A-DiT are faster. With Euler, it takes 4.25 ms, close to these single-pass policies. The encoder takes about 1.2 ms for every method, so the differences come from the action head. Longer chunks spread one call over more actions, and the time per action falls from 3.53 ms at H=1H=1 to 1.09 ms at H=16H=16.

B.2 Generalization

Fig. S1 breaks the zero-shot success of the visuomotor policies on LIBERO-plus down by perturbation type at epoch 100, as summarized in Section 6.3.

B.3 Multi-Modality

Fig. S2 shows the rollouts behind Fig. 10 for one seed. After one epoch, ODE policy already passes through all four gaps with few failures, whereas FM-DiT fails in many rollouts and mostly takes the inner routes. A2A-DiT collapses to the two inner routes throughout training. MARS covers all four routes, but many of its rollouts still fail at epoch 10.

B.4 Vision-Language-Action Model

We fine-tune π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) on the four LIBERO suites jointly (1693 demonstrations) for three epochs with one seed. All parameters are trained, including the VLM of 2.92B parameters, with AdamW, a peak learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, and a global batch size of 384 on eight A100 GPUs. Each method uses the current images of an external and a wrist camera at 224×224224\times 224 and predicts and executes chunks of 8 actions. ODE policy replaces the action expert of π0.5\pi_{0.5} (430M parameters with its projections) by a learned query that reads the image and language features of the VLM once per chunk, a FiLM-MLP vector field of four residual layers of width 512, and a gripper head, 13.7M parameters in total, all randomly initialized. As in all IL experiments, it also uses the diversity head. The proprioception enters only the field and the gripper head. The field integrates each chunk with RK4 from the end of the previous one, with the contractive perturbation (1 cm and 0.03 rad, applied to half of the training chunks). FM integrates its flow with 10 Euler steps. The VLM is pretrained in all methods, and the suffix -R only marks a randomly initialized action expert. Each LIBERO checkpoint is evaluated on the 10 fixed initial states of each task, and LIBERO-plus on the shared set of 2008 instances with one episode each. The parameters of ODE policy outside the VLM are about 3% of those of the experts, so the comparison is not at matched capacity.

Table S2 lists the success rate per suite at epoch 1. The early lead of ODE policy over the pretrained FM expert holds in all four suites and is largest on Long (92.0% vs. 81.0%). Successful episodes of ODE policy and of the pretrained FM expert take a similar number of control steps (156.7 and 156.1).

B.5 World Action Model

We fine-tune ImageWAM (Zhang et al., 2026) on the four LIBERO suites jointly (1712 demonstrations) for 10 epochs with one seed. Its image transformer (3.9B parameters) and action transformer are fine-tuned, and the text encoder is frozen. ODE policy keeps the 25 blocks of the action transformer, which read a 512-dimensional condition once per chunk through a learned query, and replaces its input, time embedding, and output layers with a FiLM-MLP vector field of four residual layers of width 512. The proprioception enters only the field. The field integrates chunks of 12 steps with Euler, with the contractive perturbation (1 cm and 0.03 rad, applied to half of the training chunks), seamless chunking, and the diversity head, and a separate head predicts the gripper. The settings that differ between the heads are listed in Table S3. LIBERO-plus uses a shared set of 2008 instances with one episode each and the same seed for all methods, and its success rate is weighted by perturbation type. All standard deviations in this subsection are over tasks, not over seeds.

Fig. S3 shows each suite. The early lead of ODE policy is largest on Spatial and Long on LIBERO, and it lasts until epoch 10 on LIBERO-plus Spatial. Table S4 lists the success rate per perturbation type. On the full LIBERO-plus set of 10030 instances, ODE policy at epoch 10 succeeds in 88.7% of the episodes, close to its 89.9% on the shared set. The baselines were not evaluated on the full set.

B.6 Real-World Experiments

We report inference cost and smoothness on the cup task of the dexterous hand in Table S5. The baselines never succeed on this task, so their measures come from failed trials and serve only as a reference. ODE policy generates a chunk 3.4 and 5.1 times faster than FM-DiT and DDIM-UNet. Its acceleration at chunk boundaries is 0.86 times that inside chunks, close to the 0.96 of the demonstrations, whereas the baselines reach 2.03 and 2.97. Its arm jerk is about one third of that of the baselines and below that of the demonstrations, as on the can task.

The pill task in Table S6 gives the same picture with a baseline that also succeeds. ODE policy generates a chunk 3.5 times faster than FM-DiT. Its ratio of the acceleration at chunk boundaries to that inside chunks is 1.45, close to the 1.24 of the demonstrations, against 2.17 for FM-DiT. Its arm jerk is half of that of FM-DiT and below that of the demonstrations, while the hand jerk of both methods is close and below that of the demonstrations.

B.7 Reinforcement Learning

We build on an open-source reproduction of SuperMimic (Liao et al., 2026a). Each iteration steps 4096 simulated environments once and stores the transitions, trains the world model on them, and updates the actor by backpropagating the discounted return over 32 steps imagined in the frozen world model, plus the value of the critic at the last step. The task is whole-body tracking of the 40 complete LAFAN1 clips (2.45 hours at 50 Hz, 100 to 300 s each) with a Unitree G1 humanoid with 29 actuated joints. The action is the offset of the joint-position targets from the default pose, tracked by a PD controller. The actor encodes the target motion into a latent 𝐳t∈ℝ32\mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{32} and decodes it with 10 frames of proprioception into the action, with 8.91M parameters. We add the anchor-relative pose of BeyondMimic (Liao et al., 2026b) to the goal for both actors, since with proprioception alone the heading drifts over such long clips and the return saturates at about 0.58.

The ODE actor keeps this network and its initialization and only reads the decoder output as the velocity in Eq. (11), where the previous action is the noise-free output of the actor, so exploration noise does not accumulate along the integration. Without bounds, the integration turned an early error of the world model into a drift of the action and a collapse of the return in one of the runs. We therefore bound the change per step by 1.62 and each joint of the action by its own limit. Both bounds are set slightly above the 99th and 99.9th percentiles of the actions of converged policies of both actors, so they are rarely active.

Everything else, including the world model, the critic, the rewards, the training noise, and the hyperparameters, follows the reproduction. Each run trains for 3 hours on one NVIDIA H200 GPU, about 33k iterations. Following SuperMimic, every clip is played once from its first frame with the deterministic policy and without noise or randomization, and an episode ends when the pelvis deviates from the reference beyond a threshold. We report the reward per step normalized by its maximum, averaged over all steps of each clip with the steps after a fall counted as zero and then over the 40 clips, and the mean squared second difference of the executed actions.

PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) uses the same environment, observations, rewards, termination conditions, domain randomization, and clips as SuperMimic, but no world model. It samples its own exploration actions, so the execution noise of the environment is turned off. Its hyperparameters follow the G1 tracking configuration of BeyondMimic (Liao et al., 2026b), with 8192 parallel environments and the network size of SuperMimic. Each run also trains for 3 hours on one H200 GPU. Since an iteration of PPO differs from one of SuperMimic, all curves are plotted over wall-clock time. Fig. S4 compares the returns of the ODE actor and PPO. The training return of PPO includes its own exploration noise and is shown only for reference.

B.8 Ablation Studies

Diversity head. The head reads the features of the field with the gradient stopped, and its loss does not reach the field, so the field receives exactly the same gradient with or without the head (Section 4.4). The head thus leaves learning unchanged and only alters the actions at inference. We evaluate the same models of three seeds without the offset (ϵ=𝟎\bm{\epsilon}=\mathbf{0}, i.e., the plain ODE), with the mean of the drawn component, and with full sampling within the component (Table S8). After one epoch, when the head is not yet trained, the offset lowers the success rate from 85.3±1.985.3\pm 1.9% to 79.8±1.679.8\pm 1.6% with component means and to 52.1±0.152.1\pm 0.1% with full sampling. From epoch 5 on, the three differ by at most 4.2 points, and full sampling even reaches the highest 94.8±0.494.8\pm 0.4% at epoch 20. The diversity head therefore mainly affects the early performance, which component means largely preserve, and we use component means for uni-modal tasks.

Vector field architecture. We replace the FiLM-MLP vector field with AdaLN Transformer blocks of FM-DiT, keeping the number of parameters (ODE-DiT, Table S7). With the Transformer, ODE policy still outperforms all baselines, with 77.2% after one epoch and 91.2% at epoch 100 (one seed), against at most 43.2% and 87.8%, and it exceeds FM-DiT with the same blocks by 5.8 points at epoch 100. However, it stays below the MLP field at every checkpoint and is much slower, training at 3.5 instead of 17.1 iterations per second and taking 51.9 instead of 11.0 ms per chunk (Table S9). Two reasons explain this. First, RK4 evaluates the field 32 times per chunk, in training as well as in execution, so the overhead of each Transformer call is multiplied. Second, the Transformer of FM-DiT models the dependencies among the actions of a chunk, whereas in ODE policy the integration already produces the chunk step by step, and the field only maps the current state to its velocity, a low-dimensional mapping that an MLP fits well. A simple MLP field is therefore sufficient, as the integration carries the temporal structure of the chunk.
